uses: Mints have been taken for digestion since the time of ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, and peppermint tea after a heavy meal is a household tradition in many places. In folk practice the leaf is brewed for wind, cramping and queasiness, and a hot cup was offered at the start of a cold. The cooling oil from the leaves has long been rubbed on the temples for a tense head. Pliny wrote that Greeks and Romans wore mint garlands at feasts and flavored their sauces and wine with it.
taste: Hot and aromatic at first, then cooling
energetics: Culpeper called garden mints hot and dry in the third degree; the menthol feels cooling
caution_pregnancy: Peppermint in food amounts is likely safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Little is known about medicinal amounts, and the EMA does not recommend medicinal peppermint leaf then. Never put peppermint oil on or near the face of a baby or young child: breathing in the menthol can affect their breathing.
caution_medications: Neither NCCIH nor the EMA names a specific drug interaction. Some herbs and medicines do interact harmfully, so ask a pharmacist before combining peppermint products with any medicine.
caution_conditions: If you have reflux or heartburn, avoid it: peppermint can make heartburn worse. People with gallstones or other bile-duct problems should be cautious. Avoid it if you are sensitive to peppermint or menthol. Medicinal leaf preparations aren't recommended for children under 4. Taken by mouth, the oil can cause heartburn, nausea, belly pain and dry mouth.
caution_duration: Peppermint tea appears safe, but the long-term safety of large amounts is unknown. The EMA advises seeing a practitioner if digestive symptoms last more than two weeks.
caution_topical: The oil can cause skin rashes and irritation. Keep it off the faces of infants and small children.
garden_harvest_timing: Cut stems just before flowering, on a dry late morning after the dew has gone; often a second cut later in the season.
notes: Spreads hard by underground runners; grow it in a pot to keep it in bounds. It rarely sets seed. Culpeper's planet is for the mints as a group (he describes spear mint), not peppermint in particular. NC State Extension notes it can upset the stomachs of cats, dogs and horses in large amounts.
